cards.prompt:
When someone else gets into your account, it's called a **take-over**. It happens to adults and big companies too. The clue: things happen that **weren't you**. Your **recovery email** is the backup that can reset your password.

Sign of a take-over, or normal?

items.label: Alert: a sign-in you didn't make
Friends got links you didn't send
Password fails, but you didn't change it
A sign-in code you didn't ask for
A recovery email you've never seen
A code while you were signing in

cards.explanation: Sign-ins, messages, codes and password changes that **weren't you** are signs of a take-over. So is a **recovery email** you don't know: whoever owns it could reset your password. A code that arrives while **you** are signing in is the account doing its job.
cards.hint: For each one, ask: did I do this, or did someone else?
cards.nudge: Alerts and codes are normal when they match something you just did. They're warning signs when they don't.

cards.title: What to do first
cards.body:
Spotted a sign? Do these first, in order:

1. **Tell a trusted adult.** You're not in trouble, and they can help you work through it.
2. **Change the password**, on a device you trust, in the real app or website. Make it new, strong and unique.
3. **Check the recovery email and phone**, and remove anything that isn't yours. Otherwise the attacker could use them to reset your new password.

cards.prompt: Put the first three steps in order.

items.label: Check the recovery email and phone

cards.explanation: **Tell a trusted adult** so you're not alone, **change the password** to lock the attacker out, then **check the recovery email and phone** so they can't reset your new password.
cards.hint: Why would checking recovery details only help **after** there's a new password?
cards.nudge: Checking the recovery details protects the new password, so the password has to be changed first.

cards.prompt: Your friends say you've been sending them strange links. You haven't.

steps.text: You can still sign in. What do you do first?

choices.text: Tell a trusted adult, and change your password
choices.consequence: Good start. The attacker's password no longer works.
You'd lose everything, and the attacker might already have your password for other sites.

choices.text: Ignore it. Friends will work it out
choices.consequence: Every hour gives the attacker more time to trick your friends.

steps.text: Your password is changed. But the attacker may **still be signed in** on their device, and a password alone could let them back in later. Two more steps help: **sign out of other devices** (in the account's security settings), and **turn on two-step sign-in**, which asks for a code from your phone as well as your password. What next?

choices.text: Check recovery details, sign out other devices, turn on two-step
choices.consequence: Whoever was in is kicked out, and a password alone can't get them back in.
The attacker may still be signed in on their device. Sign out other devices too.

steps.text: Your account is safe again. You used the **same password** on a music app too, and friends are still getting those links. What now?

choices.text: Change the music app's password, and warn friends not to click
choices.consequence: Now the old password opens nothing, and your friends know the links weren't from you.

choices.text: Leave it: only one account was hacked
choices.consequence: The attacker has that password, and they'll try it on your other accounts too. Change it everywhere you used it.

cards.explanation: Tell an adult and change the password first. Then **check the recovery details**, **sign out other devices** and turn on **two-step sign-in**. Finally, change that password anywhere else you used it, and warn your friends.
cards.hint: Is changing the password enough on its own if someone is still signed in? And where else does that old password work?

cards.prompt:
Can't get into your account at all? Use the app's official **"Forgot password"** or account recovery.

Your account was taken over. Someone messages: **"I can get it back for you for $20."** What is this?

options.text: A scam: only the app's own recovery can get it back
Real help: some people are paid experts at recovery
options.nudge: The app's own recovery is free, and nobody else can open your account for you. Think about who asks for money here.

options.text: The app's support team, who noticed the take-over
options.nudge: Real support teams don't message you asking for money. Think about who offers this for a fee.

cards.explanation: Account "recovery services" in your messages are a scam. Use the app's official **Forgot password** or account recovery, tell a trusted adult, and **never pay**.
cards.hint: The prompt says what can get you back in. Is a stranger asking for $20 part of it?

cards.prompt: You check your account's security settings.

steps.text: The **recovery email** is one you've never seen. What do you do?

choices.text: Remove it, add your own, and turn on two-step sign-in
choices.consequence: Now only you can reset the password.

choices.text: Leave it. It's only a backup
choices.consequence: The recovery email can reset your password, so whoever owns it could get back in.

cards.explanation: The **recovery email** can reset your password, so it must be yours. Remove anything you don't recognise, and add a second lock.
cards.hint: What is the recovery email used for?

cards.title: Recap
cards.body:
- Signs: anything on your account that **wasn't you**.
- First: **tell an adult**, **change the password**, **check recovery details**.
- Locked out? Use the **official recovery**. Never pay a stranger.
